title: A prayer for protection
hook: the Tenth Guru's quiet prayer asking to be sheltered

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten savaiye closed, and your line was love, not display. Did something you wear or keep carry love today? Now a new bani begins, and it's a quieter one. Day three hundred seventy.

Some prayers are made for a crowd. They're big and public, and sung by a whole hall at once. Others are made for one person, very quietly. The kind you say under your breath in the car on the way to the hospital. Or at three in the morning when the house makes a noise. Or on a plane when the wheels leave the ground. The Tenth Guru, who wrote war poetry and praise as wide as the sky, also wrote one of those. A small, close prayer. Its own heading calls it a request. Today: a prayer for protection.
screen: `PRAYERS MADE FOR A CROWD.` → `AND PRAYERS UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `THE TENTH GURU WROTE ONE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is Benti Chaupai. Benti means a humble request, the kind you make to someone greater than you, standing at their door. Chaupai is the meter, verses whose lines fall into four parts. Its heading in the Dasam Granth reads, roughly, the poet speaks: a request, in chaupai. And it's short enough to learn by heart, which many Sikhs do. It's one of the five banis of the Sikh morning, it's in the evening Rehras, and it's recited while the amrit is prepared. One honest note: Sikhs don't all stop it in the same place. Some traditions recite a longer version, some a shorter one, with a few extra verses at the end. Both are said with devotion, and this path follows the common pattern without ranking either. The prayer opens with four lines, and you can hear its whole shape in them. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. Notice what isn't there. No list of demands. No bargaining. No I'll do this if you do that. Just a hand, a heart, feet, and belonging. Over the next ten days we'll take those lines and the ones after them one at a time. And notice who is praying: a Guru who led his people through years of war. Sikhs don't hear Chaupai as a frightened prayer. They hear it as the request of someone who knew that being brave is not the same as being alone.
screen: `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `CHAUPAI: LINES IN FOUR PARTS.` · `MORNING, EVENING, AND AT AMRIT.` · `HAND, HEART, FEET, BELONGING.` · then, large: `SHELTER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first four lines. If you can, look up Chaupai Sahib in Gurmukhi or transliteration and read just the opening four lines aloud, slowly, even if you stumble on the sounds. If you can't, sit with the four ideas instead, one breath each. A hand. A heart's wish. Resting at the feet. Being taken as someone's own. Breathe in with each one and let it settle. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after the fourth. If you don't, just notice which of the four you most needed today. The bell holds the time.
Benti Chaupai. A humble request in four-part verse: the Tenth Guru's short prayer for shelter, said morning and evening and at the amrit ceremony.
Your line: shelter me. Today, when something makes you uneasy, a phone call, a bad headline, a long drive, let those two words rise up, and notice what changes. Day three hundred seventy.

screen: `DAY 370 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PROTECT ME WITH YOUR HAND.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib every morning as part of the Nitnem and again within the evening Rehras, and many also say it before travel, at night, or in times of fear.

fork.setup: you're writing a prayer for protection. you could demand, bargain, or simply ask. what does Chaupai's opening do?
options: it lists what it will give in return.
it simply asks: your hand, my heart's wish, your feet, take me as your own.
it demands that every enemy be named.
fork.reveal: the first four lines bargain for nothing. they ask for a hand, a fulfilled heart, a mind at the Lord's feet, and to be taken as the Lord's own.

original.note: Gurmukhi: benti chaupai, a humble request in chaupai verse, the poem's own heading.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer that asks for nothing bad to happen.
what it means: a humble request for shelter, a hand, belonging, from a Guru who faced danger rather than fled it.

what a scholar hears: the heading 'kabiovach benti chaupai', the poet speaks, a request in chaupai; the poem stands at the close of a long section of the Dasam Granth, and its recited length varies by tradition.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Nitnem and Rehras
